Areas here are topic groupings, and checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs. Global politics changes rapidly, so verify current examples and events against news and official sources.
sourceLabel: VCAA Australian and Global Politics study design
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Use current, specific contemporary examples in your own answers, since examiners expect recent evidence.
papers: Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.area: Key concepts and actors
points.title: Sovereignty
points.detail: The supreme authority of a state over its territory and population, the difference between internal and external sovereignty, and the pressures that erode it.

questions.q: Define sovereignty and explain two ways it is challenged in contemporary global politics.
answer: Sovereignty is the supreme authority of a state over its territory and population, free from external interference.
Internal sovereignty is authority within borders; external sovereignty is recognition as an equal by other states.
Membership of international organisations requires states to accept rules and rulings they may not prefer, limiting their freedom of action.
Transnational forces such as global capital, climate change, migration and digital communication cross borders regardless of state consent.

points.area: Key concepts and actors
points.title: The state and the national interest
points.detail: States as the primary actors, the components of national interest including security, economic prosperity and international standing.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the national interest and why states may define it differently.
answer: The national interest is what a state judges to be of greatest benefit to its people and its continued security and prosperity.
It typically includes national security, economic prosperity, regional stability and the promotion of national values or standing.
States define it differently because their geography, resources, history, alliances and domestic politics differ.
Definitions also shift with government, so the same state may pursue different priorities after an election.

points.area: Key concepts and actors
points.title: Types of power
points.detail: Hard, soft and smart power, economic and military instruments, and the relationship between capability and influence.

questions.q: Distinguish between hard power and soft power, giving an example of each, and explain smart power.
answer: Hard power is coercion through military force or economic pressure, such as sanctions, tariffs or the deployment of armed forces.
Soft power is attraction, achieved through culture, values, diplomacy and aid, so that other actors want what you want.
Smart power combines both, using coercive capability alongside attraction and legitimacy to achieve objectives.
Capability does not automatically produce influence, since a state with great military power may still fail to change another state's behaviour.

points.area: Key concepts and actors
points.title: Non-state actors
points.detail: Intergovernmental organisations, non-government organisations, transnational corporations, terrorist organisations and social movements.

questions.q: Name four types of non-state actor and explain how one of them exercises power.
answer: Non-state actors include intergovernmental organisations, non-government organisations, transnational corporations, terrorist organisations and social movements.
Transnational corporations exercise power through control of capital, employment and supply chains across many states.
They can relocate investment and production, which gives them leverage over governments seeking jobs and revenue.
They also shape regulation through lobbying and through setting de facto global standards in their industries.

points.area: Key concepts and actors
points.title: Realism and liberalism
points.detail: The competing perspectives on why states behave as they do, and what each predicts about cooperation and conflict.

questions.q: Compare realist and liberal explanations of state behaviour.
answer: Realism holds that the international system is anarchic, so states pursue power and security and can rely ultimately only on themselves.
It predicts recurring competition, arms racing and limited durable cooperation, since agreements last only while they serve state interests.
Liberalism holds that cooperation is possible and rational, through institutions, trade, law and shared democratic values that reduce the incentive for conflict.
It predicts that interdependence and international organisations can constrain states, while realists reply that such constraints fail when core interests are at stake.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: The United Nations
points.detail: The Security Council, General Assembly, Secretariat and agencies, the veto power and the debate about reform and effectiveness.

questions.q: Explain the structure of the UN Security Council and how the veto affects its effectiveness.
answer: The Security Council has five permanent members holding the veto and ten elected non-permanent members serving two-year terms.
It is the only UN body whose resolutions are binding on member states, including the authorisation of force and sanctions.
Any permanent member can block a resolution regardless of majority support, so action is impossible where a permanent member's interests are engaged.
The veto was designed to keep great powers inside the organisation, but it means the Council is least able to act precisely in the conflicts that most involve major powers.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: International law and its enforcement
points.detail: Treaties, customary law, the International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court, and the problem of enforcement without a global authority.

questions.q: Explain why international law is difficult to enforce and why states comply with it nonetheless.
answer: There is no global authority above states with the power to compel compliance, so enforcement depends on states themselves.
Courts such as the ICJ generally require state consent to jurisdiction, and judgments cannot be enforced against an unwilling great power.
States nonetheless comply most of the time because law provides predictability and reciprocity that serve their interests.
Reputation also matters, since a state known for breaking agreements finds future cooperation, trade and alliance harder to obtain.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: Regional and economic organisations
points.detail: The role of bodies such as the EU, ASEAN, the WTO and international financial institutions in shaping state behaviour.

questions.q: Explain how membership of a regional or economic organisation constrains and benefits a state.
answer: Membership requires accepting common rules, dispute mechanisms and sometimes shared decision making, which limits independent action.
States accept these constraints because access to a larger market, investment and collective bargaining power outweighs the loss of autonomy.
Organisations also provide forums for managing disputes short of conflict and for coordinating responses to shared problems.
The trade-off becomes contested when domestic groups bear the costs of compliance, which is why membership is often politically divisive.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: Non-government organisations and social movements
points.detail: How NGOs and movements influence agendas through advocacy, expertise, service delivery and mobilisation, and the limits on their power.

questions.q: Explain how NGOs influence global politics and one limitation on their influence.
answer: They shape agendas by researching and publicising issues that states would prefer to ignore, and by supplying expertise to negotiations.
They deliver services directly in areas where states are absent or unwilling, which gives them operational knowledge and legitimacy.
They mobilise public opinion, which pressures governments through domestic electorates.
Their limitation is that they hold no sovereign authority and depend on funding and access, so states can exclude, defund or ignore them.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: Transnational corporations
points.detail: Economic scale, mobility of capital, supply chains, tax practices and the relationship between corporate and state power.

questions.q: Explain the sources of transnational corporate power and how states attempt to constrain it.
answer: Their power derives from capital, employment, technology and control of supply chains spanning many jurisdictions.
Mobility allows them to shift production and profit between states, so governments compete to attract them with tax and regulatory concessions.
States attempt to constrain them through competition law, environmental and labour regulation, and coordinated international tax agreements.
Constraint is difficult because a single state acting alone risks losing the investment, which is why cooperation between states is required.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Global actors and power
points.title: Terrorist organisations and asymmetric power
points.detail: How non-state armed groups exert influence disproportionate to their resources, and the difficulties states face in responding.

questions.q: Explain why states find it difficult to respond to non-state armed groups.
answer: Such groups have no territory to defend or population to protect, so conventional deterrence has little purchase.
They operate across borders and among civilian populations, making military force imprecise and politically costly.
Their aim is often to provoke an overreaction that damages the state's legitimacy and recruits support for their cause.
Effective responses therefore require intelligence, policing, disruption of finance and addressing grievances, which are slower and less visible than force.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: Defining the region
points.detail: The Asia-Pacific and Indo-Pacific as contested geographic and strategic concepts, and the political significance of how the region is defined.

questions.q: Explain why the definition of a region such as the Indo-Pacific is itself politically significant.
answer: Defining a region determines which states are treated as central participants and which are peripheral or excluded.
The shift from Asia-Pacific to Indo-Pacific brings India into the strategic frame, which changes the balance of the grouping.
Definitions therefore reflect and advance strategic preferences rather than simply describing geography.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: The rise of China
points.detail: Economic growth, military modernisation, infrastructure investment and diplomatic initiatives, and the debate about intentions.

questions.q: Explain three instruments China uses to build influence in the Asia-Pacific.
answer: Economic instruments: trade relationships, investment and infrastructure financing create dependence and goodwill.
Military instruments: naval expansion and the construction and fortification of features in contested waters assert claims and capability.
Diplomatic instruments: bilateral agreements, regional groupings and development assistance build partnerships outside existing alliance structures.
Soft power, through cultural institutes, education and media, seeks to make Chinese leadership appear attractive rather than coercive.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: The role of the United States
points.detail: Alliance networks, forward-deployed forces, economic relationships and the debate about American commitment to the region.

questions.q: Explain how the United States exercises power in the Asia-Pacific and why regional states question its commitment.
answer: It maintains bilateral alliances and basing arrangements with partners including Japan, South Korea and Australia, providing security guarantees.
It deploys naval and air forces to assert freedom of navigation and to deter coercion.
Its economic weight and its role in international financial institutions extend influence beyond the military dimension.
Regional states question commitment because American domestic politics is volatile, priorities shift between administrations, and attention is often drawn to other regions.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: Regional flashpoints
points.detail: Maritime disputes, the Korean peninsula, Taiwan and border disputes, and the mechanisms that manage or escalate them.

questions.q: Explain why maritime disputes are difficult to resolve, using the features common to such disputes.
answer: Competing claims rest on different legal bases, including historical usage, continental shelf entitlements and exclusive economic zones.
The waters contain fisheries, hydrocarbons and major shipping routes, so the material stakes are high.
Claims are tied to national identity and domestic legitimacy, which makes compromise politically costly for any government.
International rulings can be rejected without effective enforcement, so legal processes do not settle the dispute in practice.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: Middle powers and regional groupings
points.detail: The strategies available to middle powers, including alliance, hedging and multilateralism, and the role of regional institutions.

questions.q: Explain the strategy of hedging and why middle powers in the region adopt it.
answer: Hedging means avoiding a firm commitment to one great power while maintaining useful relationships with several.
Middle powers adopt it when their security partner and their largest trading partner are strategic rivals.
It preserves economic benefit while retaining security insurance, and avoids provoking either power unnecessarily.
The risk is that as competition sharpens, both powers demand clearer alignment and the space for hedging narrows.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Power in the Asia-Pacific
points.title: Australia's regional position
points.detail: Australia's alliance relationships, economic dependence on regional trade, aid and diplomacy, and the tensions between them.

questions.q: Explain the central tension in Australia's regional strategic position.
answer: Australia's principal security relationship and its largest trading relationship are with states that are strategic competitors.
Security alignment brings intelligence sharing, technology access and deterrence, which Australia's own capabilities could not provide alone.
Economic dependence means that deterioration in the trading relationship imposes real domestic costs, as trade restrictions have demonstrated.
Australia therefore attempts to sustain both, which requires careful management and produces criticism that it is committing too far in one direction or the other.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Ethical issues and debates
points.title: Human rights
points.detail: The Universal Declaration and core treaties, the distinction between civil-political and economic-social rights, and the tension with sovereignty.

questions.q: Explain the tension between universal human rights and state sovereignty.
answer: Human rights are claimed as universal, held by all people regardless of the state they live in.
Sovereignty holds that a state's treatment of its own population is a matter of domestic jurisdiction.
When a state abuses its population, these principles conflict directly, since acting to protect rights means interfering in another state's affairs.
Some states argue that universality reflects particular cultural assumptions, though critics respond that this argument is most often used by governments seeking to escape scrutiny.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Ethical issues and debates
points.title: Humanitarian intervention and the responsibility to protect
points.detail: The doctrine that sovereignty entails responsibility, the criteria for intervention, and the record of its application.

questions.q: Explain the responsibility to protect doctrine and two criticisms of it.
answer: The doctrine holds that states have a responsibility to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity.
Where a state manifestly fails to do so, that responsibility passes to the international community, including collective action through the Security Council.
One criticism is inconsistency: intervention occurs where powerful states have interests and does not occur elsewhere, which undermines its claim to principle.
Another is that intervention can exceed its mandate and produce prolonged instability, which has made some states reluctant to authorise it again.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Ethical issues and debates
points.title: People movement and refugees
points.detail: The definition of a refugee, the principle of non-refoulement, the distinction from other migrants, and the politics of border control.

questions.q: Distinguish between a refugee and other categories of migrant, and explain the principle of non-refoulement.
answer: A refugee is a person outside their country of nationality with a well-founded fear of persecution on specified grounds who cannot obtain protection there.
Internally displaced people have fled but remain within their own country, so they fall outside the refugee definition.
Economic migrants move primarily to improve living standards and do not attract the same protection obligations.
Non-refoulement prohibits returning a person to a place where they face persecution, and is the central obligation of the refugee protection regime.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Ethical issues and debates
points.title: Development and global inequality
points.detail: Competing explanations for persistent inequality between states, and debates about aid, trade, debt and conditionality.

questions.q: Explain two competing explanations for persistent inequality between states.
answer: One explanation locates the causes internally, in governance, corruption, institutions, conflict and policy choices within poorer states.
A second locates them in the structure of the global economy, including terms of trade, debt, tariff barriers and the legacies of colonial extraction.
The two produce different prescriptions: internal explanations favour governance reform and conditional aid, structural explanations favour changing trade rules and debt relief.
Most analysts accept that both operate, and the disagreement concerns their relative weight and therefore what should be done.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Ethical issues and debates
points.title: Arms control and weapons of mass destruction
points.detail: Non-proliferation regimes, deterrence theory, verification, and the difficulty of restraining states that perceive existential threat.

questions.q: Explain why non-proliferation regimes struggle to prevent states acquiring nuclear weapons.
answer: A state that perceives an existential threat may regard nuclear weapons as the only reliable guarantee of survival.
Regimes rest on voluntary treaty commitments, and states can withdraw or refuse to join.
Verification requires intrusive inspection that states resist as an infringement of sovereignty, and civilian nuclear technology is dual-use.
Enforcement is inconsistent, since existing nuclear powers retain their own arsenals, which weakens the moral and political authority of the regime.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Climate change as a global crisis
points.detail: The collective action problem, differentiated responsibility, international agreements and the gap between commitment and implementation.

questions.q: Explain why climate change is difficult to address through international cooperation.
answer: It is a collective action problem: the benefits of mitigation are shared globally while the costs fall on the state that acts.
Every state therefore has an incentive to let others bear the cost, which weakens ambition across the board.
Responsibility is contested, since developed states produced most historical emissions while developing states argue they need growth.
Agreements rely largely on voluntary national commitments without effective enforcement, so pledges routinely exceed implementation.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Armed conflict and its changing character
points.detail: Interstate and intrastate conflict, proxy war, civil war internationalised by external intervention, and the effects on civilians.

questions.q: Explain how the character of armed conflict has changed and why this complicates international responses.
answer: Most contemporary conflict is intrastate rather than between states, involving governments, armed groups and militias.
External powers frequently intervene indirectly by supporting proxies, which prolongs conflict while avoiding direct confrontation.
Fighting occurs among civilian populations, so casualties and displacement are high and combatants are difficult to distinguish.
International mechanisms were designed largely for interstate war, so their tools of recognition, negotiation and peacekeeping fit these conflicts poorly.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Terrorism and counter-terrorism
points.detail: Definitional contestation, causes, state responses and the tension between security measures and civil liberties.

questions.q: Explain why defining terrorism is politically contested and one consequence of that contest.
answer: Definitions turn on the use of violence against civilians for political purposes, but states disagree on whether state violence is included.
Groups regarded as terrorists by one government are regarded as legitimate resistance by another, so the label is itself a political act.
No universally accepted definition exists in international law, which obstructs coordinated legal responses.
It also allows governments to apply counter-terrorism powers to domestic political opponents, which is why the definitional question has practical consequences for civil liberties.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Pandemics and global health security
points.detail: The cross-border character of disease, the role of the WHO, vaccine distribution and the tension between national and collective responses.

questions.q: Explain the tension between national and collective responses to a pandemic.
answer: Governments are accountable to their own populations, so they prioritise securing supplies and protecting citizens first.
Border closures, export restrictions and the purchase of vaccine supply beyond domestic need follow from that accountability.
Collectively, this is self-defeating, since uncontrolled transmission anywhere generates variants that cross borders regardless.
Effective collective action requires surveillance, sharing and equitable distribution, but no authority can compel states to prioritise it over domestic demands.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Economic crises and global governance
points.detail: The transmission of financial shocks, the role of international financial institutions and debates about their governance and conditionality.

questions.q: Explain how a financial crisis in one state transmits internationally and what international institutions do in response.
answer: Financial institutions hold assets and liabilities across borders, so losses in one market impose losses on institutions elsewhere.
Trade and investment links transmit the shock to the real economy, reducing demand for exports and withdrawing capital from vulnerable economies.
International financial institutions provide emergency lending to stabilise currencies and prevent default.
Such lending is usually conditional on policy changes, which is criticised for imposing austerity that deepens hardship and for reflecting the priorities of the institutions' largest shareholders.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Global crises and responses
points.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of responses
points.detail: Assessing whether a global response achieved its objectives, using criteria of authority, resources, compliance and measurable outcomes.

questions.q: Explain the criteria you would use to evaluate the effectiveness of an international response to a global crisis.
answer: Whether the response had a clear mandate and the legal authority to act, since contested authority undermines compliance.
Whether the resources committed matched the scale of the problem, as pledges frequently exceed actual disbursement.
Whether states complied in practice, which can be measured against their stated commitments.
Whether measurable outcomes improved, and whether improvement can be attributed to the response rather than to other factors.

points.area: Exam technique and case studies
points.title: Using contemporary evidence
points.detail: Supporting every claim with specific, recent and accurately dated examples rather than general assertions about global politics.

questions.q: Explain what makes evidence strong in a Global Politics response.
answer: It names the specific actors, the action taken and approximately when it occurred.
It is recent, since examiners expect contemporary evidence and the study design emphasises current global politics.
It is directly relevant to the claim being made, rather than included because it is well known.
It is accurate, since a misremembered event or date undermines the credibility of the whole argument.

points.area: Exam technique and case studies
points.title: Building an argument with perspectives
points.detail: Using realist and liberal perspectives to structure analysis, and reaching a supported judgement rather than presenting both sides neutrally.

questions.q: Explain how to use competing perspectives in an essay without simply describing both.
answer: Use each perspective to generate an explanation of the same event, showing what each makes visible.
Test both against the evidence, identifying which better accounts for what actually occurred.
Reach a judgement about which is more persuasive in this case, and explain why.
Presenting both without evaluation describes theory rather than analysing politics, and does not answer an evaluative question.

points.area: Exam technique and case studies
points.title: Command terms and mark allocation
points.detail: Matching depth to the command term and marks available, and addressing every element of a multi-part question.

questions.q: Explain how 'analyse' and 'evaluate' differ in Global Politics responses.
answer: Analyse requires breaking the issue into components and examining how they relate, showing causes, effects and interactions.
Evaluate requires weighing effectiveness, significance or validity and reaching an explicit supported judgement.
An evaluative response that stops at analysis, without stating a conclusion, cannot access the highest marks.
